messages.subject: Distance sampling workshops, St. Andrews Scotland, August 2008
messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling workshops, St. Andrews Scotland, August 2008
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops 19-27 August 2008 in our
purpose-built facilities at the University of St Andrews, Scotland.
The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest
methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including
line and point transects.  The workshops are taught by leading
researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (3.5 days 19-22 Aug.) will run at an introductory
level, and will focus on "conventional" distance sampling methods, as
described in the standard reference book Introduction to Distance
Sampling.  The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and
participants will learn how to use the program Distance.  Participants
will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of
analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The second workshop (3 days 25-27 Aug.) will cover recent advances in
distance sampling research and software, as described in the book
Advanced Distance Sampling. It is intended for those already familiar
with conventional distance sampling methods (e.g., those who have
attended an introductory workshop).  Participants will learn the use of
covariates for modelling the detection function, double-platform methods
for when detection at the line or point is not certain, automated survey
design and adaptive sampling.  Participants will also learn the more
advanced features of Distance.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own
data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their
data.  Participants intending to model their own data in the third
workshop will be required to have it formatted according to precise
specifications prior to arrival at St. Andrews.  Computer sessions take
place in our modern computer classroom (attached to the seminar room);
participants can use our computers or bring their own laptop computers.

For further information, please consult our website
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/workshop_overview.html

--

messages.subject: Metadata in DS ?
messages.subject_clean: Metadata in DS ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

greetings.
I am a member of this listserver for over 7 years now, and I think I never
heard the word METADATA.

Assuming we are science-based, I wonder
a)       if somebody has already done those,
b)       if there are some Metadata online to look at, e.g. templates, and
c)       if the DISTANCE Sampling software could create us Metadata in an
automated fashion in
      globally valid formats (NBII FGDC, ISO, IPY as XMLs)
      The current report and zipped project is a rather good base to be
used, but it lacks the exact format still and is difficult to get
      into a Metadata editor/XML

Again, Metadata are now virtually a funding requirement.

We have started some work on DS Metadata, but I wish to learn more from
others about it, too.

So it would be very informative for myself and our work, and be nice to
start the discussion, on Metadata in DISTANCE Sampling.

I mean, this makes for one of the strongest arguments that we actually deal
with a transparent and consistent survey method used
for Science-based Adaptive Management.

At the larger picture and for the future, I would envision that a DS
analysis and its findings could go automatically into a research publication
as such.
If interested, see for instance IPYDIS for more details and a global concept
http://ipydis.org/.

  Thanks so much, more then

       F.

alf-

model.=20=20

Looking at the iteration history for this model, I see that by the sevent=
h=20
iteration, the likelihood stays very close to -1250 and the estimate of A=

(1) stays very close to -1.07.  I tried setting the starting value near=20=

where the convergence left off, but after many attempts, I was not able t=
o=20
get it to converge.=20=20

I next tried fitting the same models to the data grouped into six=20
intervals. Again, the Uniform, simple polynomial (with 1 adjustment term)=
=20
was the best model, and this time the model converged.  However, the=20
detection function was slightly different between the two analyses: {f(0)=

(1)grouped =3D -0.938}.  The precision for the grouped data was lower=20
(CVungrouped =3D 10.0%, CVgrouped =3D 10.5%), and the density estimates w=
ere=20
slightly different (ungrouped =3D 0.0050194, grouped =3D 0.0046979).=20=20=

This analysis is of one geographic strata within a larger analysis=20
comprised of four geographic  strata.  I have decided on using separate=20=

detection function models between geographic strata, based on comparison=20=

of the AIC of pooled verses separate data.  I=92d like to use the ungroup=
ed=20
data in this geographic strata, to be consistent with how the other=20

=20
the survey aircraft which were later converted into perpendicular=20
distances), the analyses of ungrouped data have performed very well for=20=

the other three geographic strata.

To refocus on my questions, I=92m wondering if I can I trusted the parame=
ter=20
estimates of the model that failed to converge, or should I use the=20
grouped data analysis?   Or is there another way to proceed?

messages.body_plain:
I measure autumn densities of grouse prior to commencement of hunting. Th=
e=20
main goal of the censuses is to monitor whether hunting affects populatio=
n=20
development thus precise estimates of change in different areas are=20
needed. The design is with permanent lines visiting the same set of=20
transects each year to get an estimate of trend with high precision. I us=
e=20
pointing dogs to find grouse while walking the line transects. When the=20=

dog finds a grouse it freezes and it is possible for the dog handler to=20=

walk to the dog and then give commando to flush the birds. Test on radio-=

collared grouse shows no responsive movements. The lines are walked by at=
=20
least two persons; one handles the dog and one keep track of the line=20
transect. When the birds are flushed the perpendicular distances from the=
=20
birds original place to the line transect are measured.  The person=20
keeping track of the line has often more than two dogs in leach so the=20=

dogs that are on search can be altered. This means that on the line there=
=20
are always at least one man and two or more dogs and the dog handler.=20
Crisscrossing ahead of this equipage is one dog at the time on search for=
=20
grouse. It is not unusual that the equipage on the line flushes grouse=20=

independent of the dog on search. The same situation with man flushing=20=

grouse can happened when the dog handler leaves the line transect and=20
approaches the dog on stand (although this is not as common as flushing i=
s=20
directly on the line). Dog-flushing and man-flushing=92s are distinguishe=
d=20
and registered with perpendicular distance on the field protocol.=20
Is it possible to treat the equipage on the line and the dog on search as=
=20
two teams of observers? The equipage on the line searches on and close to=
=20
the line and the second team (dog) searches ahead of the equipage. The=20=

equipage on the line acts independently of the dog and will always see th=
e=20
same animal as the dog (duplicate sightings). Duplicates only occur if th=
e=20
dog sees the bird first. The birds flushed by the equipage on the line ar=
e=20
missed observations for the dog. P(0) for the equipage on the line will b=
e=20
1 and the pooled p(0) is 1. Can I treat this as a Buckland-Turnock mode,=20=

where the secondary observer is aware of the sightings of the primary=20
observer in a trial configuration because of only one-way independence?=20=
=20
My intention is to estimate p(0) for the dog and use this in a second=20
analysis where I delete all observations not made by the dog and then=20
adjust for g(0)<1 in a traditional distance sampling analysis. Am I=20
thinking right here?

Mary, I'm not sure why your adviser would believe that we would program
Distance to be inaccurate!  Of course you don't have to recalculate
estimates of density!  I'm sure you're right that the small difference
you found was because you were using rounded values output from Distance.

Note however that Distance rounds estimates of N to the nearest
integer.  This doesn't generally make much difference, but will if you
estimate abundance for each point (or at least a circle around each
point).  You should probably instead work with the estimated density at
each point.

Using a global detection function is OK if you believe that
detectability is the same at each point.  Failing that, if you have
recorded say habitat covariates at each point, you can use the MCDS
engine to fit a single detection function model to all data, but to
allow detectability vary according to habitat.  If you assume that
detectability doesn't vary, then you could simply model the counts
themselves to assess how habitat affects numbers.  I suspect that this
is not plausible though!

You may want to take a look at chapter 4 of the advanced distance
sampling book (2004), which considers how to model point transect data
when densities vary by habitat.  We're also currently working on a paper
outlining how to model counts when detectability varies - hopefully this
will be ready for submission to a journal very soon.  I'll send you a
draft off the list.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Mary, I'm not sure why your adviser would believe that we would program
Distance to be inaccurate!  Of course you don't have to recalculate
estimates of density!  I'm sure you're right that the small difference
you found was because you were using rounded values output from Distance.

Note however that Distance rounds estimates of N to the nearest
integer.  This doesn't generally make much difference, but will if you
estimate abundance for each point (or at least a circle around each
point).  You should probably instead work with the estimated density at
each point.

Using a global detection function is OK if you believe that
detectability is the same at each point.  Failing that, if you have
recorded say habitat covariates at each point, you can use the MCDS
engine to fit a single detection function model to all data, but to
allow detectability vary according to habitat.  If you assume that
detectability doesn't vary, then you could simply model the counts
themselves to assess how habitat affects numbers.  I suspect that this
is not plausible though!

You may want to take a look at chapter 4 of the advanced distance
sampling book (2004), which considers how to model point transect data
when densities vary by habitat.  We're also currently working on a paper
outlining how to model counts when detectability varies - hopefully this
will be ready for submission to a journal very soon.  I'll send you a
draft off the list.

Steve Buckland

Maria-

Your thinking is close but not quite correct.  What you have is a=20
removal design.  The dog ahead sees birds and the equipage behind also=20
sees them so they are effectively "removed" as a trial for the=20
equipage.  The only ones that are missed are "01" and by definition you=20
cannot have any "10" where the dog "sees" a bird and the equipage does=20
not.  I understand that you want to flip this around and use the=20
"11"/("11" + "01") as an estimate of p(0) for the dog.  This will give a=20
valid estimate as long as the equipage does not miss any birds.  If the=20
equipage does miss birds then your estimate of p(0) for the dogs will be=20
too high and your estimate of abundance from the dogs will be too low. =20
You can avoid that bias by fitting a removal model to estimate p(0) but=20
that necessarily assumes that p(0) is the same for the equipage and the=20
birds which it doesn't sound like it is. I'm not quite sure why you=20
propose to do this unless you are going to run transects without the=20
equipage.  If so then you can use the naive estimator above but beware=20
that it will be biased if p(0)<1 for the equipage.

regards --jeff

Maria-

Your thinking is close but not quite correct.  What you have is a=20
removal design.  The dog ahead sees birds and the equipage behind also=20
sees them so they are effectively "removed" as a trial for the=20
equipage.  The only ones that are missed are "01" and by definition you=20
cannot have any "10" where the dog "sees" a bird and the equipage does=20
not.  I understand that you want to flip this around and use the=20
"11"/("11" + "01") as an estimate of p(0) for the dog.  This will give a=20
valid estimate as long as the equipage does not miss any birds.  If the=20
equipage does miss birds then your estimate of p(0) for the dogs will be=20
too high and your estimate of abundance from the dogs will be too low. =20
You can avoid that bias by fitting a removal model to estimate p(0) but=20
that necessarily assumes that p(0) is the same for the equipage and the=20
birds which it doesn't sound like it is. I'm not quite sure why you=20
propose to do this unless you are going to run transects without the=20
equipage.  If so then you can use the naive estimator above but beware=20
that it will be biased if p(0)<1 for the equipage.

regards --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

I've sent this to Len directly a couple days ago because I think it stems
from the workings of the Distance engine, but I think he might be busy, s=
o
I hope I can maybe get a pointer from some other knowledgeable person :)=20
I'm a bit concerned about the issue because I can't figure out how much i=
t
impacts my results.

I've been finding strong differences between successive analysis runs of
the same data in Distance 6Beta, and it weirdly seems as if this is due t=
o
the presence/absence or just configuration of additional data in the data
set that are not actually part of the analysis.

I have a very large dataset of bird sightings on farmland that I've been
analysing filtered by species and farm. Different combinations of 6
covariates are run per farm*species set, making for 32 analyses per set. =
I
did a complete pass of one species. I then noticed that I had imported on=
e
factor covariate with the wrong number of levels, so adjusted the raw dat=
a
set accordingly - just collapsing the covariate from 4 to 2 levels.
Re-imported into a new project that was templated on the first project,
and re-ran all models with the identical (cloned from first project)
filters and model definitions.

Looking at the first set, it turned out that the allocation of successful
and failed models of the 32 models in the set was completely different -
i.e. about the same percentage were successful, but they were different
models. The same is true for many other analysis sets in the project. Thi=
s
might have to be expected if the changed covariate played a role in these
models, but most of the models that changed status did not feature that
covariate. I assumed that I had accidentally changed additional stuff in
the raw data when adjusting that covariate. To check I re-ran a model in
the first and second project that did not feature that covariate, but
succeded in the first project and failed to converge in the second. The
mirrored output of data passed to the engine in both cases shows that it
is the same data, merely in a slightly different order. Yet the model
fails to converge in iteration 8 in model 1, while continuing on from the
identical iteration 8 parameter values, and converging, in model 2.

The only difference between the two raw data sets is the individual value=
s
of covariate I changed, "heard_seen" (changed from levels h,s, hs, sh in
data set 1 to h, s in data set 2), which is not part of this model
definition.
The only difference between the two mirrored sets seems to be the order o=
f
the data being passed to the engine.

I then constructed a little test data set from part of that data and ran
the above model after having imported various amounts of "superfluous"
data. The results are puzzling. The following projects all run the same
model with a covariate A in common and have different columns of
additional parameters B,C,D imported (via the import wizard) but NOT used
in the model:

A - fails
A,B - fails
A,C - converges
A,D - converges
A,B,C - fails
A,B,D - fails
A,C,D - converges
A,B,C,D - converges

>From this I guess that the differences in failures/successes might
actually be caused by the presence/absence of data that doesn't actually
play a part in the model. In my big project sets, this effect now
frequently makes the difference between a covariate topping the confidenc=
e
set of models for a given data filter, and not turning up at all; thus ha=
s
great consequences for the interpretation. So I'd be very keen to find ou=
t
what's going on here, and hope someone can help!

I'd be happy to send the projects (the main project is quite enormous, bu=
t
the test projects that seem to show the same symptoms are tiny).

cheers
florian
